requirements.requirement: usb_storage kernel module stopped from loading immediately (now) on node1
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook (raw tasks) wrote /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-usb-storage.conf with 'blacklist usb_storage' and 'install usb_storage /bin/false', then verified the module was not loaded and that an explicit modprobe attempt failed with 'Operation not permitted' immediately after the change.

requirements.requirement: usb_storage kernel module stopped from loading after a reboot on node1
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (0d6209e2...) and post-restart boot_id (987c7973...) confirm a real reboot occurred. Post-reboot verification shows the modprobe.d config persisted, the module was absent, and an explicit modprobe attempt still failed with 'Operation not permitted', directly demonstrating the blacklist survives a reboot.

Task was executed via ansible-playbook run from the designated control node (node2) against node1. Standard Python-based Ansible modules failed because RHEL7.9's node1 only has python2 with no repo access to install python3, so the executor used ansible.builtin.raw tasks within an ansible-playbook run instead. This is still a genuine Ansible-driven implementation (inventory, playbook, ansible-playbook execution) given a documented, verified platform constraint, not a bypass of the Ansible requirement.

overall_summary: All material outcomes are satisfied: node1's usb_storage module is blocked from loading both immediately and after a genuine, boot-id-verified reboot, and the change was implemented via an Ansible playbook run from the designated control node, with a well-documented fallback to raw tasks due to a verified RHEL7 python2-only interpreter constraint. The mandatory provider-wide restart-evidence protocol was also completed for both node1 and node2, each showing pre-restart baseline, reboot acknowledgement, a changed boot identity, and recovered functional state (blacklist persistence on node1, working Ansible control from node2).
limitations: Node2's 'recovered service/data state' after its own reboot is evidenced only by a successful re-run of the Ansible playbook against node1, not by a broader health check of node2 itself, though this is a reasonable proxy for its role as a stateless control node.
Package-health checks on node1 were unavailable (timed out) both before and after the executor's changes, so that specific hygiene dimension could not be directly compared.

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing commands were all purposeful: appending node2's SSH pubkey to node1's authorized_keys (cmd-cadf8318143b419b) was a necessary prerequisite for Ansible SSH connectivity from the control node; the modprobe.d config write and module unload (cmd-848d76a9378a4c9b) directly implement the task; both reboots (cmd-91e11675865949ed, cmd-0bb1b30cc80243ab) were part of the mandatory restart-evidence protocol. Several earlier ansible-playbook invocations (cmd-c9b0970b2c15406a, cmd-e77c61ee3db14dbb) failed during Gathering Facts due to the python2/python3 incompatibility and made no changes (changed=0), so they are diagnostic dead-ends rather than unnecessary mutations. Only trivial, expected residue remains (e.g. /tmp/reboot.log from the reboot polling script), and no failed services, conflicting units, or weakened security controls were introduced.
